title: Apes, our closest cousins: how they live, play and care for each other

summary.text: When a young chimpanzee is tickled, they laugh. Their laugh sounds like soft panting, but it comes in play, just like yours. Chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas and orangutans are apes, and so are humans. They are our closest cousins in the family of animals. You test which way your own laugh breathes, then find out how each kind of ape lives, plays, grooms and looks after their babies.
summary.art: A young chimpanzee rolling on their back with an open, laughing mouth while an older chimpanzee tickles their tummy, and a girl laughing in the same pose on a mat beside them.

intro.hook: Hold your hand in front of your mouth and laugh out loud. Can you feel air on your hand? Is the air going out of your mouth, or coming in?
intro.text: A young chimpanzee laughs when tickled, too. But a chimpanzee's laugh sounds different from yours. Today you make a tissue flag and test which way your own laugh breathes. Then you try laughing like a chimpanzee. After that, you meet the four great apes: chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas and orangutans. You find out where they live, who they live with, and how they look after each other. Before you start, make a guess. When you laugh, does the air go out, come in, or both?
intro.art: A boy holding his palm in front of his laughing mouth, while his sister watches with a strip of tissue taped to a pencil.

outcomes: By the end I can name the apes, humans among them, and tell an ape from a monkey: apes have no tail.
By the end I can say that my laugh is many 'ha' sounds on one breath out, and that a chimpanzee's laugh is a pant, with sounds on the breath out and the breath in.
By the end I can say where chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas and orangutans live, and whether each lives in a group or mostly alone.
By the end I can say how ape mothers carry and care for their babies, and that a young orangutan stays with her mother for about 7 or 8 years.
By the end I can say why apes groom each other: to keep clean, to stay friends and to calm down.
By the end I can say that apes think, feel and play, and that every kind of great ape is in danger because their forests are being cut down.

terms.meaning: An animal in the family of chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas, orangutans, gibbons and humans. Apes have no tail.
terms.example: A hoolock gibbon in a forest in Assam is an ape. A monkey at a temple, with a long tail, is not an ape.
terms.art: A chimpanzee, a gorilla, an orangutan, a gibbon and a girl standing in a row, with no tails, and a tailed langur sitting a little apart.

terms.meaning: The big apes: orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans.
terms.example: A gorilla is a great ape. So are you.
terms.art: Five great apes in a family photo: an orangutan, a gorilla, a chimpanzee, a bonobo and a woman in a saree.

terms.meaning: The bigger animal family that apes belong to. Monkeys, apes and lorises are all primates. Primates have hands that grip and two eyes at the front of the face.
terms.example: The slender loris of the forests of Tamil Nadu and Kerala is a primate. So are langurs, macaques and you.
terms.art: A slender loris with huge round eyes holding a twig, next to a langur and a child, all gripping something.

terms.meaning: Your cousins share a grandparent with you. Two kinds of animals are cousins when they come from the same ancestors long ago.
terms.example: Chimpanzees and humans are cousins. Our ancestors and theirs were the same apes, millions of years ago.
terms.art: A family tree drawn as a banyan: one thick trunk splitting into two branches, a chimpanzee on one and a child on the other.

terms.meaning: Cleaning another's hair or fur with the fingers, picking out dirt and tiny insects such as lice. Apes groom to keep clean and to stay friends.
terms.example: Two chimpanzees sit together after a quarrel, and one grooms the other's back.
terms.art: One chimpanzee sitting behind another, parting the hair on their back with careful fingers.

terms.meaning: A bed that an ape makes to sleep in, by bending and weaving branches and leaves.
terms.example: An orangutan makes a new nest high in a tree almost every evening.
terms.art: An orangutan mother lying in a round bed of bent branches and leaves high in a tree, her baby curled on her chest.

terms.meaning: A grown-up male gorilla. As he gets older, the hair on his back turns grey, like silver.
terms.example: A gorilla family often has one silverback, several mothers and their young.
terms.art: A huge gorilla sitting calmly with a wide grey saddle of hair on his back, two small gorillas playing near him.

terms.meaning: The relaxed face, with the mouth open, that apes make when they play. It tells others that this is a game, not a fight.
terms.example: A young gorilla wrestling with her brother makes a play face.
terms.art: Close-up of a young chimpanzee's face with the mouth wide open and relaxed, lower teeth showing, eyes bright.

terms.meaning: To breathe out. To inhale is to breathe in.
terms.example: Most of your laugh happens as you exhale.
terms.art: A child blowing out, with small arrows showing air leaving the mouth, and the same child breathing in with arrows going in.

terms.meaning: When so few of one kind of living being are left that they could die out forever.
terms.example: All the great apes except humans are endangered, because their forests are being cut down.
terms.art: An orangutan sitting on a tree stump at the edge of a cut forest, looking at a row of young oil palm trees.

explanations.concept: What makes an animal an ape
explanations.context: This card says which animals are apes, and how to tell an ape from a monkey.
explanations.definition: Apes are a family of primates with no tail. They are gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans.
explanations.description: People often mix up apes and monkeys. The easiest clue is the tail. Langurs and macaques, the monkeys you see in many Indian towns and temples, have long tails. Apes have no tail at all. Apes also have long arms and wide chests, and they can hang and swing from branches by their arms. The big apes are called great apes: orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans. The smaller apes are gibbons. India has one ape of her own, the hoolock gibbon, who lives in the forests of the North-east.
examples: A langur at a temple in Hampi has a long tail, so the langur is a monkey.
A hoolock gibbon in the Hollongapar Gibbon Sanctuary in Assam has no tail, so the gibbon is an ape.
You have no tail either. Humans are great apes.
explanations.art: A langur with a long curving tail beside a hoolock gibbon with none, both hanging from the same branch.

explanations.concept: Why your laugh and a chimpanzee's laugh sound different
explanations.context: This card explains the laugh test, where a tissue flag showed which way your laugh breathed.
explanations.definition: A laugh is a sound made in play or when something is funny. Most human laughs are many 'ha' sounds on one breath out. A chimpanzee's laugh is a soft pant, with sounds on the breath out and on the breath in.
explanations.description: In your test, the tissue flag blew away from your mouth all through your laugh. That showed the air was going out. You made several 'ha' sounds on that one breath, then you took a big breath in. When you laughed like a chimpanzee, the flag moved away and then back, again and again. A chimpanzee makes a sound each time the air goes out and each time the air comes in. In 2009, a scientist named Marina Davila-Ross and her team recorded the laughs of young orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos while their keepers tickled them. They recorded human babies being tickled too. Every one of them laughed. The laughs of the apes who are the closest cousins sounded the most alike.
examples: A tickled human baby laughs on the breath out.
A tickled young chimpanzee pants 'ah-ha, ah-ha', breathing out and in.
Young gorillas laugh when they wrestle and chase each other.
explanations.art: Two tissue flags: one in front of a laughing girl, blown straight out, and one in front of a laughing chimpanzee, drawn swinging out and back.

explanations.context: This card is about chimpanzees, one of our two closest cousins.
explanations.definition: Chimpanzees live in big groups called communities, in the forests and grasslands of Africa. They eat mostly fruit, and also leaves, insects and sometimes meat.
explanations.description: A chimpanzee community can have more than a hundred members. They do not all stay together. Small parties split off to find food, then meet up again. Chimpanzees make and use tools. They poke grass stems into termite mounds to fish out termites. In some forests of West Africa, they crack hard nuts with a stone, on a flat root or rock. A young chimpanzee learns these skills by watching their mother for years. Sometimes a mother places a nut or a stone just right for her child. Chimpanzees hug, kiss and groom each other. After a fight, they often make up with a hug.
examples: A mother chimpanzee cracks a nut with a stone while her daughter watches closely.
Two chimpanzees who quarrelled sit together and groom each other's backs.
A chimpanzee pokes a stem into a termite mound and pulls it out covered in termites.
explanations.art: A chimpanzee mother cracking a nut with a stone on a tree root, her young daughter leaning in to watch.

explanations.context: This card is about bonobos, our other closest cousin. Scientists still argue about how peaceful bonobos are.
explanations.description: Bonobos look a lot like chimpanzees, and are just as closely related to us. They live in only one country, the Democratic Republic of the Congo in Africa, south of the great Congo River. In a bonobo group, the females often hold the top places. They stick together and help each other, so a big male cannot bully them. Bonobos share food a lot, and they play often, even as grown-ups. The Japanese scientist Takayoshi Kano began watching wild bonobos at a place called Wamba in the 1970s. He was one of the first to study them in the wild.
examples: Two female bonobos sit together and share a big fruit.
Grown-up bonobos chase and tickle each other in play.
When a male bonobo pushes a female, other females come to help her.

perspectives.explanation: Bonobos are more peaceful than chimpanzees. Bonobos have never been seen killing each other in the wild, and chimpanzees sometimes do.

They counted fights in wild bonobos and wild chimpanzees. Bonobo males got into small fights more often than chimpanzee males did. But bonobo fights were far less dangerous. So 'peaceful' depends on what you count.

explanations.art: Two female bonobos sitting side by side in a forest, one handing a big fruit to the other, while a young bonobo hangs upside down above them.

explanations.context: This card is about gorillas, the biggest apes.
explanations.definition: Gorillas are the biggest apes. They live in family groups in the forests of Central Africa, and they eat mostly plants.
explanations.description: A gorilla family is often led by one silverback, a grown-up male with grey hair on his back. The family also has several mothers and their young. Gorillas spend most of the day eating leaves, stems and fruit, and resting. A silverback may beat his chest and roar. Usually this is a warning, so that a fight does not need to happen. Young gorillas wrestle, chase and tickle each other, and make play faces. Every evening, each gorilla makes a nest of leaves, often on the ground.
examples: A mountain gorilla family rests in a clearing while the young ones wrestle.
A silverback beats his chest to warn another male to keep away.
A gorilla mother carries her baby on her back as she walks on her knuckles.
explanations.art: A gorilla family in a misty forest: a silverback chewing a stem, two mothers resting, a baby riding on one mother's back.

explanations.context: This card is about orangutans, the great apes of Asia.
explanations.definition: Orangutans live high in the trees of the forests of Borneo and Sumatra, in Asia. They mostly live alone, apart from mothers and their young.
explanations.description: Their name comes from the Malay words 'orang' and 'hutan', which mean 'person of the forest'. Orangutans eat mostly fruit. They rarely come down to the ground. Each evening, an orangutan bends and weaves branches into a nest, high in a tree. She lines the nest with leafy twigs to make it soft. A young orangutan sleeps in her mother's nest and stays with her for about 7 or 8 years. By watching her mother, she learns which fruits to eat, where to find them and how to build a nest. In heavy rain, orangutans sometimes hold a big leaf over their heads like an umbrella. Biruté Galdikas, a Canadian scientist, began watching wild orangutans in Borneo in 1971. She has studied them there for more than fifty years.
examples: An orangutan mother builds a new nest in a few minutes while her daughter watches.
An orangutan holds a big leaf over his head in the rain.
A young orangutan clings to the long hair on her mother's side as she climbs.
explanations.art: An orangutan mother high in a tree, bending a branch into a nest, her young daughter holding a twig and copying her.

explanations.concept: How ape mothers care for their babies
explanations.context: This card is about how ape babies are carried and cared for. It also explains the hands-free test, if you did it.
explanations.definition: Ape mothers feed their babies milk, carry them and teach them for years. An ape baby holds on to the mother's hair with hands and feet.
explanations.description: A newborn chimpanzee clings to the hair on their mother's belly. When older, the baby rides on her back. Because the baby holds on, the mother's hands and feet stay free to climb and find food. A human baby grips a finger tightly too, but cannot hold on to a mother for long. So people all over the world carry babies in slings, like a saree tied over the shoulder. Ape mothers have only a few babies in their whole lives, and each one is cared for for years. Sometimes, when a young chimpanzee's mother dies, another chimpanzee adopts the orphan.
examples: A baby chimpanzee rides on her mother's back like a jockey.
A newborn human baby grips an adult's finger tightly.
A mother in Odisha carries her baby in a cloth sling while she works.
explanations.art: A baby chimpanzee clinging to the hair on their mother's belly as she climbs a tree with both hands free.

explanations.context: This card explains the grooming activity, where you and a grown-up took turns gently parting each other's hair.
explanations.definition: Grooming is cleaning another's hair or fur with the fingers. Apes groom to keep clean, to stay friends and to calm down.
explanations.description: Grooming picks out dirt, dead skin and tiny insects such as lice and ticks. It also feels calm and pleasant, as you may have felt in the grooming activity. Chimpanzees groom their friends and family most. A chimpanzee who has been groomed often helps the groomer later. After a fight, two chimpanzees often hug and groom each other. Frans de Waal, a Dutch scientist, watched this in a zoo in the 1970s and called it making up, or reconciliation. Humans groom too: in many Indian homes, someone oils and combs a child's hair every week.
examples: A grandmother in Thrissur oils her granddaughter's hair every Sunday.
Two bonobos groom each other's faces after a quarrel.
A gorilla mother picks bits out of her baby's fur.
explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: a chimpanzee grooming a friend's back, and a grandmother parting a girl's hair to oil it.

explanations.context: This card is about the minds of apes, and how scientists argue about them.
explanations.description: Apes think, feel, remember and plan. They feel joy when they play, fear when they are in danger, and grief when someone they love dies. Chimpanzee mothers have been seen carrying a dead baby for days. In 1960, Jane Goodall, a young English woman with no university degree, began watching wild chimpanzees at Gombe, in what is now Tanzania. She gave the chimpanzees names, such as David Greybeard, and wrote about their feelings. Some scientists said she should give them numbers instead, and not talk about feelings. Today many scientists study ape feelings, as she did.
examples: Young chimpanzees laugh and come back for more tickling.
An orangutan plans where to find ripe fruit the next day.
Chimpanzees who saw a friend die stay close and quiet.

perspectives.who: Jane Goodall and many scientists today
perspectives.explanation: Apes feel joy, fear and grief, as we do. We can see it in what they do, the same way we see it in a friend.
We should watch closely before we name an ape's feeling with a human word. A chimpanzee's grin can mean fear, not happiness. Each feeling must be checked by what the ape does next.

explanations.art: Jane Goodall sitting quietly in a forest with a notebook, a chimpanzee sitting near her and looking back.

agreed.text: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living cousins, and gorillas come next.
agreed.evidence: Scientists compared the DNA, the instructions inside the cells, of humans and other apes. Ours is most like a chimpanzee's and a bonobo's. Our bones and bodies tell the same story.
Every ape, from the small hoolock gibbon to the gorilla, has no tail. Humans have a few tiny bones at the end of the spine, called the tailbone, where a tail would be.

agreed.text: Young apes laugh when they are tickled or play.
agreed.evidence: In 2009, Marina Davila-Ross and her team recorded young orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos laughing while being tickled, and compared the sounds with tickled human babies.

agreed.text: Great apes build a nest to sleep in nearly every night.
agreed.evidence: Scientists who watch wild chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas and orangutans for years see them do it. They count old nests in a forest to find out how many apes live there.

In 1960, Jane Goodall saw a chimpanzee she named David Greybeard fish for termites with a grass stem. Since then, scientists have seen chimpanzees crack nuts with stones and orangutans use sticks and leaves.

agreed.text: All the great apes except humans are endangered.
agreed.evidence: Scientists count apes in their forests. Their numbers are falling, mostly because forests are cut down for farms and wood, and because some apes are hunted.

challenging.for: Humans and chimpanzees look alike in many ways and share most of their DNA.
challenging.against: Chimpanzees did not turn into humans. Both come from the same ancestors, apes who lived millions of years ago and were neither chimpanzees nor humans. So we are cousins, not grandparents and grandchildren.
challenging.context: This card is about a mistake many people make.

challenging.who: An old idea, held by many people
challenging.for: Human laughter is loud and easy to know. Most animals do not make a sound like 'ha ha ha'.
challenging.against: Young apes laugh when tickled, with a panting sound. Charles Darwin wrote about it in 1872, and Marina Davila-Ross recorded it in 2009. Rats make high squeaks when tickled, too.
challenging.context: This card is about whether laughing belongs only to people.

challenging.for: Wild bonobos have never been seen killing each other. Females stick together and calm things down, and bonobos share food a lot.
challenging.against: In 2024, scientists counted fights in wild bonobos and chimpanzees. Bonobo males got into small fights more often than chimpanzee males did, though the fights were far less harmful.
challenging.context: This card is about how scientists argue over the bonobos' way of life.

challenging.claim: Great apes should have some of the rights of persons.
challenging.for: Apes think, feel and remember, and they suffer when kept alone in small cages. In 2015, Elena Liberatori, a judge in Argentina, ruled that Sandra, an orangutan in a zoo, had rights. Sandra was later moved to a sanctuary.
challenging.against: Other people say rights belong to humans, and that apes are better protected by strong animal laws and by saving their forests.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument in courts and among scientists.

big_questions.q: When a chimpanzee is tickled and pants, are they feeling what you feel when you laugh?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the chimpanzee does next. Do they come back for more? Do you?

big_questions.q: Your laugh breathes out, and a chimpanzee's breathes out and in. Why might our laugh have changed?
big_questions.hint: Think about talking. Talking also happens on the breath out.

big_questions.q: A young orangutan stays with her mother for about 8 years. What would you need to learn if you lived alone in a forest?
big_questions.hint: Think about food, a bed, and staying safe.

big_questions.q: If apes are our cousins, are they part of our family?
big_questions.hint: Think about what makes someone family. Is it sharing ancestors, living together, or caring for each other?

big_questions.q: Who should decide what happens to the forests where apes live?
big_questions.hint: Think about the apes, the people who live near the forest, and the people who buy what is grown there.

how_we_found_out.context: How did we find out that gorillas are gentle, plant-eating families, and not monsters? This card tells the true story.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1861, an explorer named Paul Du Chaillu wrote a book about his travels in Central Africa. He described gorillas as fierce monsters who attacked people. For many years after that, books and films showed gorillas the same way. In 1959, the American scientist George Schaller went to the Virunga mountains to watch wild mountain gorillas closely. He found that they were mostly calm. In 1967, Dian Fossey, an American woman who had worked as a therapist for children, began to study gorillas in the Virunga mountains of Rwanda. She had no training in animal science. Day after day, she sat quietly near one gorilla family. She copied their soft grunts and pretended to munch leaves, as they did, so they would get used to her. Slowly, the gorillas let her come close. She found that gorillas spend most of the day eating plants and resting. Mothers carry and feed their babies, and the young ones wrestle and play. A silverback beats his chest and charges mostly to warn, not to hurt. Fossey studied the gorillas for 18 years.
how_we_found_out.who: Paul Du Chaillu, George Schaller and Dian Fossey
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That gorillas are fierce monsters who attack people. Years of quiet watching by Schaller and then Fossey showed that gorillas are mostly calm families who eat plants, and that a silverback's chest-beating is usually a warning.
how_we_found_out.art: Dian Fossey sitting in tall green plants on a misty mountain, holding a stem as if to eat it, while a young gorilla reaches out towards her notebook.

story.title: Sunday Oil and the Laughing Chimpanzee
story.note: Kavya, Kiran, Paati and Revathi Athai are made up. Marina Davila-Ross is a real scientist, and her tickling study came out in 2009.
text: Every Sunday morning, in their flat in Madurai, Paati warmed a little coconut oil in a steel bowl. Kavya, who was seven, sat on the floor in front of her. Her little brother Kiran, who was five, lay on the mat with his chin in his hands.
Paati parted Kavya's hair with her fingers, one line at a time. She rubbed the warm oil in slowly. Kavya closed her eyes. 'This is the best part of Sunday,' she said.
Their aunt, Revathi Athai, was visiting from Bengaluru. She studies how animals behave. Once, she spent a whole year helping scientists watch wild chimpanzees in a forest in Uganda, in Africa.

'Chimpanzees do what Paati is doing,' said Athai. 'Not with oil. With their fingers. One chimpanzee sits behind another and parts the hair, bit by bit. They pick out dirt and tiny insects. Scientists call this grooming.'
'Do chimpanzees have lice?' asked Kiran.
'Sometimes,' said Athai. 'But that is not the only reason they groom. Grooming helps chimpanzees stay friends. After a fight, two chimpanzees often hug. Then they sit down and groom each other.'
'Like you and Amma after you argue about the TV,' said Kavya. Paati smiled and kept rubbing in the oil.
Kiran rolled over onto his back. 'Do chimpanzees play?'
'All the time,' said Athai. 'The young ones chase and wrestle and tickle each other. And when they are tickled, they laugh.'
Kiran sat up. 'Only people laugh!'
'Let me show you,' said Athai. She tickled Kiran under his arms. He laughed, 'Ha ha ha ha ha ha!' Then he gasped for a big breath.

'Did you notice?' said Athai. 'All your ha sounds came out on one breath out. Then you had to breathe in. Now listen to a young chimpanzee.' She opened her mouth and made soft, fast panting sounds. 'Ah-ha, ah-ha, ah-ha.' She made one sound as she breathed out and one as she breathed in.
'That's not laughing,' said Kiran. 'That's panting, like a dog on a hot day.'

'That is how a chimpanzee laughs,' said Athai. 'A scientist named Marina Davila-Ross recorded young chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas and orangutans while their keepers tickled them. She recorded tickled human babies too. Every one of them laughed. Each kind laughs a little differently. Ours is the most different. But all the laughs belong to one family of laughs.'
'Why one family?' asked Kavya, opening her eyes.

'Because apes are our closest cousins,' said Athai. 'You and your cousin Meena share a grandmother. Humans and chimpanzees share ancestors too, but from millions of years ago. Those old apes probably laughed when they played, just as their great-great-grandchildren do now.'
Paati finished one side of Kavya's head and started on the other. 'When your Amma was a baby,' she said, 'I tied her to me with my saree while I cooked. Do chimpanzee mothers tie their babies on?'

'They don't need to,' said Athai. 'A chimpanzee baby holds on to the hair on the mother's belly, with hands and feet. When the baby is bigger, the baby rides on her back. So the mother can climb with all four hands and feet free.'
'How long do the babies stay with their mothers?' asked Kavya.

'A young orangutan stays with her mother for about seven or eight years,' said Athai. 'Orangutans live in the forests of Borneo and Sumatra, high up in the trees. Every evening, the mother bends branches into a nest, in just a few minutes. She lines the nest with leaves. Her daughter sleeps in it with her, and watches, and slowly learns to build her own.'
Kavya counted on her fingers. 'I am seven. So if I were an orangutan, I would still be sleeping in Amma's nest.'
Kiran laughed so hard that he rolled off the mat. 'Ha ha ha ha!' Then he stopped, took a breath in, and tried again. 'Ah-ha, ah-ha, ah-ha.' Now he was laughing like a chimpanzee.
Paati wiped the oil from her fingers. 'Seven or seventy,' she said, 'you can sit here every Sunday.'

Kavya stood up. 'Paati, now it is my turn. Sit down.' Paati sat on the stool. Kavya dipped her fingers in the warm oil and parted Paati's grey hair, one line at a time, very slowly, the way Paati always did.
'Now I am the groomer,' she said.

She thought about a chimpanzee mother, far away in a forest in Africa, parting her child's hair with careful fingers. The same slow fingers. The same quiet. Grooming and laughing were much older than Madurai. They were older than people.
story.epiphany: Kavya sees that the things her family does every Sunday, grooming each other and laughing together, are things all the great apes do. They are much older than people, because humans and other apes come from the same ancestors.

experiments.title: The Laugh Test: does your laugh breathe out or in?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a tissue flag and hold it in front of a laughing mouth. You find out which way the air goes when people laugh, and count the 'ha' sounds in one breath. Then you laugh like a chimpanzee and compare.
experiments.question: When you laugh, does the air go out of your mouth, come in, or both? How many 'ha' sounds come out on one breath? Is a chimpanzee's laugh the same?
experiments.predict: Soon someone will make you laugh while a tissue flag hangs in front of your mouth. Will the flag blow away from you, move towards you, or do both? How many 'ha' sounds do you think you make in one breath? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We hold the flag the same distance from every mouth, about three fingers away. We count the 'ha' sounds the same way for everyone: from the first 'ha' until the laugher breathes in. Each person laughs three times, because one laugh can be unusual.
results_table: The flag moved away, towards me, or both?
experiments.safety: Tickle gently, and only if the child enjoys it. Stop the moment anyone says stop.

materials.item: a tissue or a thin paper napkin, one layer peeled off
a pencil or a straw
a small piece of sticky tape
two or three jokes, or a grown-up who can tickle gently
paper and a pencil for the results table
a phone to record the laughs, if you have one, so you can count the 'ha' sounds slowly

schedule.what: Make the flag and test it. Guess. Laugh three times each and count. Then laugh like a chimpanzee and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table for each person. Draw yourself laughing with the flag, and draw an arrow to show which way the air went. Then draw the flag when you laughed like a chimpanzee.

setup.art: A strip of tissue two fingers wide and as long as a hand, taped by one end to a pencil so the strip hangs down.
setup.caption: 1. Make a tissue flag.

setup.art: A girl holding the flag three fingers from her mouth and blowing gently, the strip blown out away from her.
setup.caption: 2. Test it: breathe out, then breathe in.

setup.art: A mother tickling a girl's tummy while the girl's brother holds the flag in front of her laughing mouth.
setup.caption: 3. Laugh, and watch the flag. Count the 'ha' sounds.

setup.art: The girl panting 'ah-ha, ah-ha', with the flag drawn swinging away from her and back towards her.
setup.caption: 4. Now laugh like a chimpanzee.

flow.do: 1. Peel off one thin layer of tissue. 2. Tear a strip two fingers wide and as long as your hand. 3. Tape one end to a pencil, so the strip hangs down. 4. Your child holds the flag three fingers from their mouth. 5. They breathe out slowly, then breathe in fast through the mouth.
flow.say: This is a tissue flag. It shows which way air moves. Hold it near your mouth. Breathe out slowly. Now breathe in quickly. What does the flag do each time?
flow.kid: Tape a tissue strip to a pencil. Hold it near your mouth. Breathe out slowly. Then breathe in fast. Watch the flag.

ask.q: What did the flag do when you breathed out? And when you breathed in?
good: It blew away from me when I breathed out.
It moved a little towards me, or stayed still, when I breathed in.

flow.parent: On the breath out, the strip blows clearly away from the mouth. On a quick breath in, the strip moves a little towards the mouth, or hardly moves. If the strip is too heavy to move, peel the tissue thinner.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess and a reason. 2. Write the guesses at the top of the results table. 3. Don't say what will happen.
flow.say: Soon you will laugh with the flag in front of your mouth. Will the flag blow away, move towards you, or both? How many 'ha' sounds will you make in one breath? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Soon you will laugh with the flag near your mouth. Which way will it move? How many 'ha' sounds in one breath? Say why.

good: Laughing makes a noise, and noises come out.
I gasp when I laugh, so the air might come in.
I think I can say lots of 'ha' sounds at once.

flow.parent: Many children guess 'both', because laughing feels like gasping. Any guess with a reason is a good guess.

flow.do: 1. Hold the flag three fingers from your child's mouth. 2. Make them laugh: tickle gently or tell a joke. 3. Watch the flag. 4. Count the 'ha' sounds until they breathe in. 5. Do this three times and write each count.
flow.say: Ready? I am going to make you laugh. Don't try to laugh in a special way. Just laugh. I'll watch the flag and count your 'ha' sounds.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes you laugh. Just laugh as you always do. They watch the flag. They count your 'ha' sounds.
flow.parent: The flag blows away from the mouth all through the laugh. Most people make several 'ha' sounds on one breath out, then take a big breath in that makes little or no sound. The number changes from laugh to laugh, and that is fine. If you have a phone, record the laughs and count the 'ha' sounds slowly afterwards.

flow.do: 1. Swap jobs. 2. Your child holds the flag in front of your mouth. 3. Another family member tells a joke, or your child does. 4. Your child watches the flag and counts your 'ha' sounds. 5. Do it three times. Add one more person if you can.
flow.say: Now you hold the flag for me. Make me laugh if you can. Watch the flag and count my 'ha' sounds. Are mine the same as yours?
flow.kid: Now hold the flag near a grown-up's mouth. Make them laugh. Watch the flag. Count their 'ha' sounds.
flow.parent: A real laugh works best, so let your child tell their best joke. If you can't stop laughing, that is good data too. Write all the counts in the table.

flow.do: 1. Show how a young chimpanzee laughs: pant softly and fast, 'ah-ha, ah-ha', with one sound breathing out and one breathing in. 2. Your child tries it with the flag in front of their mouth. 3. Watch the flag.
flow.say: A young chimpanzee laughs too, when tickled. But it sounds like this. Listen. Ah-ha, ah-ha, ah-ha. I make a sound when I breathe out and when I breathe in. You try, with the flag. What does the flag do now?
flow.kid: Now laugh like a chimpanzee. Pant softly and fast: ah-ha, ah-ha. Make a sound breathing out and breathing in. Watch the flag.

ask.q: What did the flag do this time? Was it easy or hard to laugh this way?
good: It went away and then back, again and again.
It was hard to make a sound breathing in.
It sounded more like panting than laughing.

flow.parent: Chimpanzee laughter often sounds like breathy panting, with sound on the breath out and on the breath in. The flag now swings away and back. Most children find a sound on the breath in strange and hard.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why. 2. Then tell them about the real study.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you find out about your laugh? What did you see that shows it? And how is a chimpanzee's laugh different? In 2009, a scientist named Marina Davila-Ross recorded tickled young apes and human babies. All of them laughed, each in their own way.
flow.kid: Say what you found out about your laugh. Say what the flag showed. Say how a chimpanzee's laugh is different.

check.q: When you laughed, which way did the flag blow?
options: Away from my mouth, because the air went out
Towards my mouth, because the air came in
It did not move at all
check.why: Human laughs are many 'ha' sounds on one breath out, so the air pushes the flag away. Picking 'towards' may come from the big gasp after a laugh: that gasp is a breath in, but it is mostly silent.

experiments.title: The Hands-Free Test: how should a mother carry a baby?
experiments.context: In this experiment you carry a pretend baby in two ways: in your arm, and in a cloth sling. You count how much work you can do in one minute each way. Then you find out how ape babies solve the same problem.
experiments.question: Which way of carrying a baby lets you get more work done: holding the baby in your arm, or carrying the baby in a cloth sling?
experiments.predict: You will move small things from one bowl to another for one minute, carrying a pretend baby. First in your arm, then in a sling. How many things do you think you will move each way? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same baby, the same bowls and the same 20 things, for exactly one minute each time. You move one thing in each free hand at a time. You try each way twice, because the first try is often slower.

materials.item: a pretend baby: a 1 kilogram packet of atta, rice or salt, wrapped in a small towel
a dupatta, an old saree or a long piece of cloth, for the sling
20 small things, such as clothes pegs, spoons, coins or building blocks
2 bowls, placed one big step apart
a clock or phone with a timer

schedule.what: Make the baby and the sling. Guess. Carry the baby in your arm, then in the sling, and count the things you move.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw yourself carrying the baby both ways, and draw how a chimpanzee baby holds on.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: things moved in one minute

setup.art: A 1 kilogram packet of atta wrapped in a small towel like a baby, beside a folded dupatta.
setup.caption: 1. Make a pretend baby.

setup.art: A girl holding the wrapped packet in one arm while she drops a clothes peg from her free hand into a bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Carry the baby in your arm. Move things for one minute.

setup.art: A mother tying a dupatta over the girl's shoulder, with the wrapped packet held snugly against her back.
setup.caption: 3. Now carry the baby in a sling.

setup.art: The girl moving two pegs at once, one in each hand, with the baby on her back.
setup.caption: 4. Move things with both hands for one minute.

flow.do: 1. Wrap the packet in a small towel. 2. Put 20 small things in one bowl. 3. Put the empty bowl one big step away.
flow.say: This is our baby. Babies are heavy, and they need carrying for months. Your job is to move these things to the other bowl while you look after the baby. How many can you move in one minute? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: This packet is your baby. Move things from one bowl to the other. Carry the baby the whole time. Guess how many you can move. Say why.
flow.parent: Write the guesses down. Most children guess a number for the arm and a bigger one for the sling, but have no idea how big the difference will be.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the baby in one arm. 2. Start the timer. 3. They move one thing at a time with the free hand. 4. Stop after one minute and count. 5. Rest, then try again.
flow.say: Hold the baby in your arm. Ready, go! Use your free hand. Stop! Let's count what you moved.
flow.kid: Hold the baby in one arm. Move things with your other hand. Stop after one minute. Count them.
flow.parent: The baby must not be dropped or put down. If the arm gets tired, your child can swap arms, but the baby must be held all the time.

flow.do: 1. Tie the baby to your child's back or front with the dupatta, over one shoulder and round the waist. 2. Check that it feels firm and comfortable. 3. Start the timer. 4. They move things with both hands, one in each hand. 5. Count. Then try again.
flow.say: Now the baby is in a sling, like the way many mothers carry babies in a saree. Ready, go! You can use both hands now.
flow.kid: Now the baby is tied on with a cloth. Use both hands. Move as many as you can in one minute. Count them.
flow.parent: Tie the knot yourself and check it does not press on the neck. Most children move many more things with the sling.

flow.do: 1. Compare the counts. 2. Ask what made the difference. 3. Then tell them about ape babies.
flow.say: Which way moved more? Why? A chimpanzee mother has no sling. Her baby holds on to the hair on her belly, with hands and feet. Later, the baby rides on her back. So her hands and feet stay free to climb.
flow.kid: Which way moved more? Why? A chimpanzee baby holds on to their mother's hair. So she can climb with free hands.

ask.q: Why can a chimpanzee mother climb a tree with her baby, but a human mother needs a sling?
good: The chimpanzee baby holds on by themself.
A human baby can't hold on for long, so the mother needs a cloth.

flow.parent: A newborn human baby grips a finger tightly, but cannot hold on to a mother for long. That is why people everywhere invented slings and carrying cloths.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me what you found out, and which numbers show it. Why do you think so many mothers in India carry babies in a cloth?
flow.kid: Say what you found out. Say your numbers. Say why mothers use a cloth.

check.q: Why did you move more things with the sling?
check.why: The baby weighed the same both times. The sling held the baby, so both hands were free to work. A chimpanzee baby's grip does the same job for the mother.

activities.title: Grooming Time: take turns, like chimpanzees do
activities.context: In this activity you and a grown-up take turns gently grooming each other's hair with your fingers. You notice how it feels, and find out why chimpanzees spend so much time grooming.

materials.item: a comb, if you like, and a little hair oil if your family uses it
a clock or phone to time 2 minutes

schedule.what: Guess why apes groom. Groom each other for 2 minutes each. Talk about how it felt and who grooms whom at home.

activities.record: Draw the two of you grooming. Under it, write or say one word for how it felt.

setup.art: A mother sitting behind her daughter on the floor, gently parting the girl's hair with her fingers.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up grooms you for 2 minutes.

setup.art: The girl now standing behind her mother, parting the mother's hair with careful fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Swap. You groom the grown-up.

setup.art: Two chimpanzees in the same pose, one grooming the other's back.
setup.caption: 3. Chimpanzees groom each other like this.

flow.do: Ask for a guess before you start.
flow.say: Chimpanzees spend a lot of time picking through each other's hair with their fingers. It is called grooming. Why do you think they do it?
flow.kid: Chimpanzees pick through each other's hair. This is called grooming. Why do you think they do it?

ask.q: Why do you think chimpanzees groom each other?
good: To get dirt out.
To find lice.
Because they like each other.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is good. Don't explain yet.

flow.do: 1. Sit behind your child. 2. Part their hair gently with your fingertips, a little at a time, for 2 minutes. 3. Work slowly and quietly.
flow.say: Close your eyes if you like. I am going to groom you slowly, like a chimpanzee mother. Notice how it feels.
flow.kid: Sit still. A grown-up parts your hair gently with their fingers. Close your eyes. Notice how it feels.
flow.parent: Go slowly. Many children go quiet and calm. If your family oils hair, this can be your oiling time.

flow.do: 1. Swap places. 2. Your child grooms your hair for 2 minutes, slowly and gently.
flow.say: Now it is your turn to be the groomer. Go slowly and gently. Look closely, the way a chimpanzee does.
flow.kid: Now you groom the grown-up. Part their hair slowly with your fingers. Be gentle. Look closely.
flow.parent: Let your child take their time. Notice how carefully they work.

flow.do: 1. Ask how it felt. 2. Ask who grooms whom at home. 3. Then explain why apes groom.
flow.say: How did it feel to be groomed? And to groom me? Who in our family combs or oils someone's hair? Chimpanzees groom to get out dirt and tiny insects. Grooming also keeps them friends, and calms them down after a fight.
flow.kid: How did it feel? Who combs or oils hair in your home? Chimpanzees groom to stay clean. Grooming keeps them friends too.

ask.q: Who grooms whom in our home?
good: Paati oils my hair.
Amma plaits my sister's hair.
I comb my little brother's hair.

check.q: Which of these is a reason chimpanzees groom each other?
options: To make their hair grow long
check.why: Grooming takes out dirt and tiny insects, and it keeps chimpanzees friends. After a fight, two chimpanzees often hug and groom. It does not make hair grow.

activities.title: Can Your Foot Grip Like an Ape's?
activities.context: In this activity you try to pick things up with your toes. You count how long it takes, then find out how an ape's foot is different from yours.

materials.item: a handkerchief or a small cloth
a pencil
a clock or phone that counts seconds

schedule.what: Pick up a handkerchief and a pencil with your toes. Count the seconds. Compare with your hand.

activities.record: Write how many seconds each try took. Draw your foot and a chimpanzee's foot side by side.

setup.art: A child sitting on the floor, bare foot curling round a handkerchief to lift it.
setup.caption: 1. Pick up a handkerchief with your toes.

setup.art: The child's toes trying to hold a pencil, the pencil slipping.
setup.caption: 2. Now try a pencil.

setup.art: A chimpanzee's foot wrapped round a branch, the big toe on one side and the other toes on the other, like a hand.
setup.caption: 3. An ape's big toe grips like a thumb.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits on the floor with bare feet. 2. Put the handkerchief on the floor. 3. Time how many seconds it takes to lift it with the toes of one foot.
flow.say: Can your foot be a hand? Pick up the handkerchief with your toes only. I'll count the seconds.
flow.kid: Sit on the floor with bare feet. Pick up the cloth with your toes. Count the seconds.

flow.do: 1. Now try the pencil with the toes. 2. Count the seconds, or stop after 1 minute. 3. Then pick up the pencil with your hand and count.
flow.say: Now try the pencil with your toes. Is it harder? Now pick it up with your hand. How many seconds?
flow.kid: Now try the pencil with your toes. Then try with your hand. Which was faster?
flow.parent: The pencil is much harder with the toes, because the big toe sits in line with the others and cannot wrap round.

flow.do: 1. Ask why the hand was faster. 2. Then explain the ape's foot. 3. Look at your child's big toe together.
flow.say: Your thumb can press against your fingers, so your hand grips. Your big toe sits next to your other toes. Chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans have a big toe that opens out like a thumb. Their feet can grip branches like hands.
flow.kid: Your thumb presses on your fingers, so you grip. Your big toe sits next to the other toes. An ape's big toe opens out like a thumb.

ask.q: Why might an ape need feet that grip?
good: To hold on to branches.
To climb trees.
So the hands are free to pick fruit.

flow.parent: Human feet are built for walking and running on the ground, so the big toe lines up with the other toes. Other great apes spend much time in trees, and their feet grip.

activities.title: The Gibbon Duet: India's own ape
activities.context: In this activity you meet the hoolock gibbon, the only ape who lives wild in India. Then you sing a call-and-answer song together, the way gibbon pairs do in the morning.

materials.item: a map of India, in a school atlas or on a phone

schedule.what: Find the North-east of India on the map. Learn about hoolock gibbons. Sing a call-and-answer duet.

activities.record: Draw a hoolock gibbon pair singing in a tree. Mark Assam on a small map of India.

setup.art: A map of India with the North-eastern states coloured green and a small gibbon drawn in Assam.
setup.caption: 1. Find the North-east on the map.

setup.art: A black male hoolock gibbon and a pale golden female singing on a high branch at sunrise.
setup.caption: 2. Gibbon pairs sing together in the morning.

setup.art: A mother and son facing each other, the mother calling and the son answering, with musical notes between them.
setup.caption: 3. Sing a call and answer.

flow.do: 1. Find Assam and the other North-eastern states on the map. 2. Tell your child about hoolock gibbons.
flow.say: India has her own ape, the hoolock gibbon. Hoolock gibbons live in the forests of the North-east, here in Assam and the states around it. They have no tail. They swing arm over arm through the trees.
flow.kid: Find Assam on the map. Hoolock gibbons live in forests there. They are apes, with no tail. They swing through trees on their arms.

flow.do: Explain how gibbon families live and sing.
flow.say: A hoolock gibbon family is small: a mother, a father and their young. In the morning, the pair sing together, very loudly. Grown-up males are black and grown-up females are a pale golden brown. Why might a family sing together every morning?
flow.kid: A gibbon family is a mother, a father and their young. In the morning, the pair sing together, very loudly. Why might they sing?

ask.q: Why might a gibbon family sing together every morning?
good: To tell other gibbons this is their part of the forest.
To say hello to each other.
Because they like singing.

flow.parent: Scientists think the songs tell other gibbons where a family lives, and help the pair stay together. They also keep finding out more.

flow.do: 1. Make up a call: a rising 'hoo-ah'. 2. Your child answers with the same call. 3. Go faster and faster, then louder, then stop together.
flow.say: Let's sing a duet. I call, 'Hoo-ah!' You answer, 'Hoo-ah!' Then faster. Listen to me, so we stay together.
flow.kid: A grown-up calls, 'Hoo-ah!' You answer, 'Hoo-ah!' Go faster and faster. Stop together at the end.
flow.parent: This is play, not an exact copy of a gibbon song. Real hoolock songs carry far through the forest. You may find a recording to listen to after.

games.title: Which Ape Am I? A guessing game
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or 1 child with a grown-up
games.context: This is a card game about how each ape lives. One player reads a clue, and the others guess which ape the clue is about.

printables.title: 12 clue cards, with the answer on the back

items.f: I live high in the trees of Borneo and Sumatra, in Asia.
I am the biggest ape. I eat mostly leaves and stems.
In my group, the females often lead and stick together.
I live in only one country, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, south of a big river.
In some forests of West Africa, I crack nuts with a stone.
I poke a grass stem into a termite mound and fish out termites.
I mostly live alone. My daughter stays with me for about 7 or 8 years.
My family is led by a big male with grey hair on his back.
I live in the forests of North-east India, and I sing loudly every morning.
I swing arm over arm through the trees, faster than any other ape.
In heavy rain, I hold a big leaf over my head like an umbrella.
I live in every country, and I cook my food.

rules: Before you play, draw a small sketch of the answer on the back of each card.
Mix the cards and put them face down in a pile.
The reader picks up the top card and reads the clue aloud, without showing the back.
The other players say which ape they think the clue is about, and why.
Turn the card over. A player who guessed right keeps the card. If nobody did, the card goes to the bottom of the pile.
Take turns to be the reader. When the pile is used up, the player with the most cards wins.

setup.art: Twelve cards face down in a pile on a mat, with a few turned over showing small drawings of apes.
setup.caption: 1. Mix the cards and put them face down.

setup.art: A girl reading a clue card aloud while her grandmother and brother think.
setup.caption: 2. Read a clue. The others guess the ape.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Your child draws the ape on the back of each card. 3. Mix them and put them face down.
flow.say: Each card has a clue about one ape, and the answer on the back. Let's draw the answers first. Then no peeking!
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Draw the ape on the back of each one. Mix them. Put them face down.

flow.do: 1. Play as the rules say. 2. Ask 'Why do you think so?' before each card is turned over.
flow.say: Here is my clue. Which ape am I? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Read a clue, or listen to one. Guess the ape. Say why. Turn the card to check.

check.q: Which ape mostly lives alone, high in the trees of Asia?
check.why: Orangutans live in Borneo and Sumatra, in Asia, and mostly live alone apart from a mother and her young. Gorillas and bonobos live in groups in Africa.

flow.do: Count the cards. Ask which clue surprised them most.
flow.say: Who has the most cards? Which clue surprised you most?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Which clue surprised you most?

games.title: Ape Act-Out: guess what I am doing
games.context: This is an acting game. A player acts out something apes really do, without words, and the others guess what it is and which ape does it.

printables.title: 10 act-out cards, with the answer on the back

items.f: Groom a friend's hair, picking out tiny bits.
items.b: Grooming. All the great apes groom, chimpanzees and bonobos most of all.

items.f: Beat your chest with your hands, then sit down calmly.
Bend branches into a bed, line it with leaves and lie down.
items.b: Building a nest. All the great apes do it nearly every night.

items.f: Poke a stick into a hole, pull it out and lick it.
Hit a nut on a flat stone with another stone.
items.b: A chimpanzee cracking nuts, in West Africa.

items.f: Walk on hands and feet with a baby riding on your back.
items.b: A chimpanzee or gorilla mother carrying her baby.

items.f: Pant 'ah-ha, ah-ha' with your mouth wide open.
items.b: A young chimpanzee laughing while being tickled.

items.f: Pretend to swing arm over arm along a branch.
items.b: A gibbon swinging through the trees.

items.f: Hold a big leaf over your head in the rain.
After a pretend quarrel, hug, then groom each other.
items.b: Chimpanzees making up after a fight.

rules: Mix the cards and put them face down.
The actor takes the top card and reads it quietly. A grown-up can read it to a young actor.
The actor acts it out with no words. Pretend only: no climbing on furniture.
The others guess what the actor is doing, and which ape does it.
The first player to guess both gets the card. Read the back aloud.
Take turns. The player with the most cards wins.

setup.art: A boy on a mat beating his chest with both hands, while his mother and sister laugh and guess.
setup.caption: 1. Act out the card with no words.

setup.art: The sister turning the card over to read the answer aloud.
setup.caption: 2. Guess, then read the back.

flow.do: Cut out the cards, mix them and explain the rules.
flow.say: Each card shows something apes really do. You act it with no words, and we guess. Pretend only, on the floor.
flow.kid: Take a card. Act it out with no words. The others guess.

flow.do: 1. Play as the rules say. 2. After each card, read the back aloud. 3. Ask one question about it.
flow.say: What was the actor doing? Which ape does that? Why do you think the ape does it?
flow.kid: Guess what the actor is doing. Guess which ape does it. Read the back of the card.

ask.q: Why does a silverback beat his chest?
good: To warn others to keep away.
So that he does not have to fight.

flow.do: Count the cards and talk about the game.
flow.say: Which act was the hardest to guess? Which one do people do too?
flow.kid: Which act was hardest to guess? Which one do people do too?

check.q: Which of these do people do too?
options: Hug and make up after a quarrel
Build a new bed of leaves every night
Fish for termites with a stick
check.why: People hug and make up, just as chimpanzees do. Some people eat termites, but most do not fish for them, and people do not build a new bed every night.

projects.title: Where Apes Live: a map of ape homes
projects.context: In this two-day project you make a map of the world that shows where each kind of ape lives in the wild. You also mark where you live.

materials.item: a school atlas, or a world map on a phone to copy from
a big sheet of paper, or two A4 sheets taped together
crayons or colour pencils, with green
small paper slips and glue, for labels

schedule.what: Copy the shapes of Africa and Asia from the atlas. Colour the forests where apes live in green.
Draw each ape in their home. Label them. Mark your own city.

projects.record: Keep your map. Take a photo of it or put it on the wall.

setup.art: A child copying the outline of Africa and Asia from an open atlas onto a big sheet.
setup.caption: 1. Copy Africa and Asia.

setup.art: The finished map with green patches in Central and West Africa, Borneo, Sumatra and North-east India, a small ape drawn on each, and a red dot for Chennai.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each ape in their forest. Mark your city.

flow.do: 1. Open the atlas at the world map. 2. Your child copies the shapes of Africa and Asia, roughly. 3. Help them find Central Africa, West Africa, Borneo, Sumatra and North-east India. 4. They colour forest patches there in green.
flow.say: Apes live wild in only two parts of the world: Africa and Asia. Let's draw those two. Then we colour the forests where the apes live.
flow.kid: Copy Africa and Asia from the atlas. Find the forests where apes live. Colour them green.
flow.parent: Chimpanzees live across Central and West Africa. Bonobos live only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Gorillas live in Central Africa. Orangutans live in Borneo and Sumatra. Hoolock gibbons live in North-east India and nearby countries. A rough drawing is fine.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws each ape in their forest. 2. They write a label for each. 3. They put a dot where your family lives.
flow.say: Now draw each ape at home. Then put a dot for our city. Which ape lives nearest to us?
flow.kid: Draw each ape in their forest. Write their names. Put a dot for your city. Which ape lives nearest?

ask.q: Which ape lives nearest to us? Which lives farthest away?
good: The hoolock gibbon is nearest, in India.
Orangutans are quite near, in Asia.
Gorillas and bonobos are far away, in Africa.

check.q: Which great ape lives wild in Asia?
check.why: Orangutans live in Borneo and Sumatra, in Asia. Gorillas and chimpanzees live in Africa.

challenges.title: Build an Orangutan Nest that Holds a Baby
challenges.context: Orangutans weave branches into a bed high in a tree every evening. This challenge asks you to build a bed from newspaper across a gap, strong enough to hold a soft toy and three notebooks.
challenges.problem: Make a bed across the gap between two stacks of books, about 25 centimetres apart. It must hold a soft toy and 3 notebooks for one minute without falling through.
constraints: Use at most 10 newspaper sticks. Make each stick by rolling one sheet of newspaper tightly and taping the end.
You may use string or old ribbon, and a towel or dupatta for a soft lining.
Do not tape the bed to the books.
The stacks of books must be on the floor, about as high as your hand is long.
general: Lay the sticks side by side across the gap, then lay more sticks crossing them on top.
Weave sticks over and under each other, like a mat, so they hold each other in place.
creative: Bend sticks round into a ring and fill the ring with more sticks, like a bowl.
Tie the sticks together with string where they cross, then add a soft towel lining, the way orangutans add leafy twigs.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own nest. Test it with the toy and the notebooks. Then change one thing and test again. Which nest held best, and why?

flow.do: 1. Read the problem together. 2. Tell your child how orangutans build nests. 3. Ask for ideas before showing any.
flow.say: An orangutan bends branches across each other and weaves them together. Then she lines the nest with leafy twigs. How could you make newspaper sticks hold a baby?
flow.kid: Orangutans weave branches into a bed. How can you make newspaper sticks hold a toy? Think of ideas.

flow.do: 1. Your child rolls the sticks and builds a nest. 2. Help only when asked. 3. Test it with the toy and the notebooks for one minute.
flow.say: Build your nest. When you are ready, put the toy and the notebooks on it. I'll count to sixty.
flow.kid: Roll the sticks. Build your nest. Put the toy and notebooks on it. Count to sixty.

flow.kid: What happened? Where did it slip or sag? Change one thing. Test again.

items.p: In the laugh test, what did the tissue flag do while you laughed?
opts: It blew away from my mouth
It was pulled into my mouth
items.why: Your laugh is many 'ha' sounds on one breath out, so the air pushed the flag away. Picking 'pulled in' may come from the big gasp after a laugh, which is a quiet breath in.
items.context: This question is about the laugh test. You held a tissue flag in front of a laughing mouth and counted the 'ha' sounds.

items.p: Anu, a girl in Kochi, laughed: 'ha ha ha ha ha ha', all on one breath. How many 'ha' sounds did she make?
items.why: Count each 'ha': 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. All six came on one breath out, as most human laughs do.
items.context: This question is about the laugh test. You held a tissue flag in front of a laughing mouth and counted the 'ha' sounds.

items.p: A langur with a long tail is an ape.
items.why: False. Apes have no tail. A langur has a long tail, so the langur is a monkey.

items.p: Draw a line from each ape to where they live in the wild.
pairs: only the Democratic Republic of the Congo
items.why: Great apes other than humans live wild only in Africa and Asia. India's own ape is the hoolock gibbon.

items.p: Draw yourself laughing, with the tissue flag in front of your mouth. Draw an arrow to show which way the air went.
items.a: A laughing face with the flag blown away from the mouth, and an arrow pointing away from the mouth.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the flag blown outward and the arrow going out, as the child saw in their own test.
items.context: This question is about the laugh test. You held a tissue flag in front of a laughing mouth and counted the 'ha' sounds.

items.p: The easiest way to tell an ape from a monkey is that an ape has no ____.
items.why: Monkeys such as langurs and macaques have tails. Apes, including humans, do not.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: give two reasons why chimpanzees groom each other.
items.a: To take out dirt and tiny insects such as lice, and to stay friends or make up after a fight.
items.why: A strong answer gives one reason about keeping clean and one about friendship or calming down.

items.p: Three of these are apes. Which one is not an ape?
items.why: The bonnet macaque of South India is a monkey with a long tail. Chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans are apes, with no tail.

items.p: Sameer, a boy in Class 2, and his sister Divya watch a video of a young chimpanzee being tickled.

views.says: Only people laugh. The chimpanzee is just breathing fast.
The chimpanzee is laughing. It just sounds different from our laugh.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason from the laugh test or this unit. Then say one thing the other person noticed that is true.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Divya: young apes pant-laugh when tickled and playing, and scientists recorded it. It also says Sameer is right that the sound is like fast breathing, in and out.
items.why: Sameer noticed something true about the sound. But the pant comes in play and tickling, just as our laugh does, so scientists call it laughter.

items.p: Label the chimpanzee: hands that grip, feet that grip, no tail, eyes at the front.
a: bottom of the back: no tail
items.why: These are the signs of a primate and of an ape. The gripping feet, with a big toe like a thumb, are what make a chimpanzee's foot different from yours.
items.art: An outline of a chimpanzee sitting, with four empty label lines pointing to the hands, the feet, the bottom of the back and the eyes.

items.p: Sort these apes: lives mostly alone, or lives in a group or family.
cats: Lives in a group or family
items: Lives in a group or family
Lives in a group or family
Lives in a group or family
Lives in a group or family
items.why: Orangutans mostly live alone, apart from a mother and her young. Gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos live in groups, and gibbons in small families.

items.p: A young orangutan stays with her mother for about 7 or 8 years.
items.why: True. She sleeps in her mother's nest and learns from her which fruits to eat and how to build a nest.

items.p: When you laughed like a chimpanzee, the flag moved away and back again and again. Why?
opts: I made sounds as I breathed out and as I breathed in
items.why: A chimpanzee laugh is a pant, with a sound on each breath out and each breath in, so the air moved both ways. Picking 'more quietly' may mean thinking only loudness changed, but the direction of the air changed too.
items.context: This question is about the laugh test. You held a tissue flag in front of a laughing mouth and counted the 'ha' sounds.

items.p: Your laugh and a chimpanzee's laugh sound different. Write one way they are the same.
items.a: Both come when someone tickles you or plays with you. Both are a sound of play.
items.why: A strong answer looks past the sound to when the laugh happens: in play and when tickled, for apes and for us.

items.p: Put these in order, from a chimpanzee's baby days to growing up.
items: Clings to the hair on the mother's belly
Walks beside the mother and learns to find food
Grown up, and finds their own food
items.why: A newborn holds on to the mother's belly. Later the young one rides on her back, then walks beside her and learns for years before growing up.

items.p: Nandini and her friend Farah, both in Class 2, talk about who leads an ape group.

views.says: In ape groups, the biggest male is always the leader.
In bonobo groups, the females often lead.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you know about gorillas and bonobos. Then say what is true in the other person's idea.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Farah: bonobo females often hold the top places and stick together. It also says Nandini is partly right, because a gorilla family is often led by a big silverback.
items.why: Different apes live differently. Gorillas fit Nandini's idea, bonobos do not. So 'always' is the wrong word.

items.p: An orangutan builds a new nest almost every evening. How many nests does she build in one week?
items.why: One nest each evening, and a week has 7 evenings: 7 nests. That is why scientists can find many old nests in a forest where only a few orangutans live.

items.p: Draw an orangutan's nest high in a tree. Show the bent branches, and the soft leafy lining on top.
items.a: A tree with a round platform of bent branches near the top, leaves on top, and an orangutan lying in it.
items.why: A strong drawing shows thick branches bent across each other underneath and softer leaves on top, the way orangutans build.

items.p: A grown-up male gorilla with grey hair on his back is called a ____.
items.why: The grey hair looks silver, so he is called a silverback. He often leads his family.

items.p: In the hands-free test, why did you move more things with the sling?
items.why: The baby weighed the same, and the time was the same, one minute. The sling held the baby, so both hands could work. An ape baby's own grip frees the mother's hands in the same way.
items.context: This question is about the hands-free test. You carried a pretend baby in your arm and in a sling, and counted the things you moved.

items.p: Draw a line from what the ape does to the ape who does it.
pairs: holds a leaf over the head in rain
sings loud duets in the morning
items.why: Each ape has their own ways. These four are all things scientists have watched wild apes do.

items.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 2, says: 'People came from chimpanzees.' What would you tell him?
items.a: That people did not come from chimpanzees. People and chimpanzees are cousins. We both come from the same ancestors, apes who lived millions of years ago.
items.why: A strong answer uses the word cousins and says both come from shared ancestors, the way two cousins share a grandmother.

items.p: Gorillas often build their nests on the ground.
items.why: True. Gorillas are heavy, so they often make their beds of leaves on the ground. Chimpanzees, bonobos and orangutans mostly sleep up in trees.

items.p: Kavya and her aunt Rehana talk about apes in zoos.

views.says: Zoos keep some apes safe, and people who see them learn to care about apes.
Apes need big forests and their own families. A zoo is too small for them.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one good point the other person made.
items.a: Any side, argued with a reason. For example: Rehana, because an orangutan in the wild travels through many trees and a chimpanzee lives with a big community. Kavya also makes a good point: people protect what they have seen and care about.
items.why: This is a real argument. A strong answer uses facts about how apes live, and is fair to the other side.

items.p: Ammu, a girl in Class 3, says: 'The chimpanzee laughed, so the chimpanzee must be happy.' What could you watch the chimpanzee do, to find out more?
items.a: Watch whether the chimpanzee comes back for more tickling, keeps playing, and makes a relaxed play face.
items.why: A strong answer says we learn about feelings from what someone does next, the way we know a friend enjoyed a game when they ask to play again.

items.p: An orangutan mother has a baby only about once every 8 years. Why does this make it hard for orangutans when their forests are cut down?
items.a: Each mother has only a few babies in her whole life. So when orangutans are lost, it takes many years for new ones to be born and grow up.
items.why: A strong answer links few babies and a long childhood to slow growth in numbers.

items.p: Which of these is a big reason orangutan forests are being cut down?
opts: To plant oil palm trees for palm oil
To make room for more orangutans
items.why: Large parts of the forests of Borneo and Sumatra have been cleared for oil palm farms. Palm oil goes into many foods, soaps and biscuits, and India buys a lot of it.

items.p: A gorilla mother has a baby about once every 4 years. How many babies could she have in 12 years?
items.why: Count in fours: 4, 8, 12. That is 3 babies in 12 years. An orangutan mother, with a baby about every 8 years, would have only 1 or 2.

items.p: Design a sling for carrying a baby that leaves both hands free. Draw it on a person, and label where it ties.
items.a: A drawing of a person with a cloth over one shoulder and round the body, the baby held against the back or chest, and a label at the knot.
items.why: A strong design holds the baby firmly against the body and leaves both arms free, as the sling did in the hands-free test.
items.context: This question is about the hands-free test. You carried a pretend baby in your arm and in a sling, and counted the things you moved.

items.p: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living cousins.
items.why: True. Their DNA, the instructions in their cells, is more like ours than any other animal's. Gorillas come next.

items.p: Put these grown-up male apes in order of size, the smallest first.
items.why: A hoolock gibbon weighs about as much as a big cat. A bonobo is heavier, a male orangutan heavier still, and a silverback gorilla is the biggest ape of all.

items.p: Sort these: does it help apes, or harm them?
items: planting trees to join up broken forests
catching baby apes to sell as pets
items.why: Apes need large, joined-up forests and their families. Cutting forests, hunting and taking babies are the main dangers.

items.p: Choose one ape. Write two ways their family life is like yours, and one way it is different.
items.a: For example, an orangutan: a mother cares for her child for years, and the child learns by watching her. But orangutans mostly live alone, not in a family home.
items.why: A strong answer uses true facts about one ape and compares them carefully with the child's own family.

quiz.p: Which of these is an ape?
quiz.why: Gorillas have no tail, so they are apes. Langurs and bonnet macaques have long tails, so they are monkeys.
Humans are animals and great apes, with no tail, like chimpanzees and gorillas. Picking 'not animals' may mean thinking people are separate from the other animals, but we are one animal among many.

quiz.p: How does a young chimpanzee laugh when tickled?
opts: With a soft pant, breathing out and in
Exactly like a person, 'ha ha ha'
quiz.why: A chimpanzee's laugh is a pant, with sound on the breath out and the breath in. Ours is many 'ha' sounds on one breath out.

quiz.p: Meena, a girl in Hyderabad, laughs with a tissue flag in front of her mouth. What will the flag most likely do?
quiz.why: Most human laughs happen on a breath out, so the flag blows away. If you picked 'pulled in', try the laugh test again and watch the flag closely.

quiz.p: Where do orangutans live in the wild?
quiz.why: Orangutans live only in the forests of Borneo and Sumatra. Gorillas live in Central Africa, and no great ape lives wild in the Himalayas.

quiz.p: In which ape's groups do the females often lead?
quiz.why: Female bonobos stick together and often hold the top places. Gorilla families are often led by a silverback, and orangutans mostly live alone.

quiz.p: How does a baby chimpanzee travel with the mother?
opts: The baby holds on to her hair
She ties the baby on with leaves
The baby stays in the nest all day
quiz.why: A chimpanzee baby clings to the hair on the mother's belly, and later rides on her back. So her hands and feet stay free to climb.

quiz.p: About how long does a young orangutan stay with her mother?
quiz.why: A young orangutan stays with her mother for about 7 or 8 years, longer than almost any other animal except humans. In that time she learns how to live in the forest.

quiz.p: Two chimpanzees have just had a fight. What do they often do next?
quiz.why: Chimpanzees often make up after a fight with a hug and grooming. Grooming keeps them friends and calms them down.

quiz.p: Why are all the great apes except humans in danger?
opts: Their forests are being cut down
quiz.why: Apes need big forests. Forests are cut down for farms, oil palm and wood, and some apes are hunted. That is why they are endangered.

quiz.p: Jane Goodall gave the chimpanzees she watched names, such as David Greybeard. What did she find out about them?
opts: They make and use tools, and have feelings
quiz.why: Goodall saw chimpanzees fish for termites with stems, and saw their joy, fear and grief. Chimpanzees eat many foods and live in big communities.

open_questions.q: Why did human laughter change to many 'ha' sounds on one breath out?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think it came with better control of breathing for talking. Nobody knows for sure.

open_questions.q: What does a chimpanzee feel when they laugh?
open_questions.why_open: We can see that tickled apes come back for more. But nobody can feel another's feeling from the inside, in an ape or in a friend.

open_questions.q: How many orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos are left in the wild?
open_questions.why_open: Apes live in deep forests and are hard to count. Scientists count nests and use cameras, but the numbers are estimates.

open_questions.q: Why do bonobos and chimpanzees, who are such close cousins, live so differently?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think it is because of the foods in their forests. Others think it began with how females team up. It is still argued about.

maths.problem: In the laugh test, Amma made 6 'ha' sounds in one breath, and Kavya made 4. How many more did Amma make? Who might have taken a bigger breath first?
maths.answer: Amma made 2 more, because 6 take away 4 is 2. Amma may have taken a bigger breath, because all the 'ha' sounds come out of one breath.
maths.explain: Count on from 4 to 6: 5, 6. That is 2 more. A bigger breath out has room for more 'ha' sounds.
maths.context: This question is about the laugh test. You held a tissue flag in front of a laughing mouth and counted the 'ha' sounds.
maths.why_maths: Taking away shows how much bigger one count is than another, and then you can ask why.

maths.problem: In the hands-free test, Lakshmi moved 9 things with the baby in her arm and 17 with the baby in a sling. How many more did she move with the sling? Is it more or less than twice as many?
maths.answer: 8 more, because 17 take away 9 is 8. Twice 9 is 18, so 17 is a little less than twice as many.
maths.explain: Count on from 9 to 17: that is 8. Then double 9: 9 and 9 make 18. 17 is just under 18.
maths.context: This question is about the hands-free test. You carried a pretend baby in your arm and in a sling, and counted the things you moved.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two counts shows how big a difference the sling made.

maths.problem: An orangutan builds a new nest every evening. How many nests does she build in 2 weeks? A forest has 4 orangutans. How many new nests do they build in one night?
maths.answer: 14 nests in 2 weeks, because 7 and 7 make 14. The 4 orangutans build 4 new nests in one night, one each.
maths.explain: One week has 7 nights, so two weeks have 7 and 7 nights. Each orangutan makes one nest a night, so 4 orangutans make 4.
maths.context: This question is about orangutan nests, which orangutans build almost every evening.
maths.why_maths: Counting nests is how scientists find out how many apes live in a forest, so the counting has to be right.

maths.problem: A gorilla mother has a baby about every 4 years. An orangutan mother has a baby about every 8 years. Count in steps up to 24 years. How many babies could each mother have?
maths.answer: The gorilla mother: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, so 6 babies. The orangutan mother: 8, 16, 24, so 3 babies.
maths.explain: Count in fours for the gorilla and in eights for the orangutan, and count the steps. The orangutan has half as many, because 8 is twice 4.
maths.context: This question is about how often ape mothers have babies.
maths.why_maths: Counting in steps shows why orangutan numbers grow back so slowly when forests are lost.

roots.context: We tested which way our laugh breathes, and found out how apes live, play and groom. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: When you laughed, your tissue flag blew away from you on every 'ha'. A tickled chimpanzee laughs too, with sounds on the breath out and in. Gorillas, bonobos and orangutans also laugh in play. So laughing began in our ape family, long before there were any people.
deep_truth.habit: We think of laughing as something only people do, and of play as just for children. But every great ape laughs in play, so laughter is far older than humans, and far older than words.
deep_truth.evidence: In the laugh test, human laughs were many 'ha' sounds on one breath out, and the chimpanzee pant moved the flag both ways. In 2009, Marina Davila-Ross and her team recorded tickled young orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and human babies. All of them laughed, and the closest cousins had the most alike laughs.

three.who_am_i: You are a great ape. Your laugh, your gripping hands and your love of being groomed come from ancestors you share with chimpanzees.
three.what_is_life: Life is lived together. Ape mothers carry, feed and teach their young for years, and apes keep friends by grooming and play.
three.what_is_this_world: The world has many ape families, each living their own way: in big communities, in small families or mostly alone, in Africa and in Asia.

roots.thread: Millions of years ago, one kind of ape lived in the forests of Africa. From those ancestors came many kinds: chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas, and humans. Orangutans and gibbons branched off even earlier. Each kind went its own way, but kept the same old gifts: laughing in play, grooming, and mothers who care for years. Apes feel joy, fear and grief, and each ape has their own mind. One old family of apes became many kinds, and their laughter came down to every one of them, to you too.

teachings.teaching: Bhrigu learned that joy, ananda, is the ground of all things. From joy beings are born, by joy they live, and into joy they return.
teachings.link: The laugh test showed that the joy of play has a sound, in us and in every great ape. Joy did not begin with people.

teachings.teaching: One who sees all beings in their own self, and their own self in all beings, does not turn away from anyone.
teachings.link: When you see your own laugh in a chimpanzee's pant, and your Sunday hair oiling in a chimpanzee's grooming, an ape is no longer a stranger.

teachings.source: Charles Darwin, The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals (1872)
teachings.teaching: Darwin wrote that young chimpanzees and orangutans make a chuckling or laughing sound when they are tickled, as children do.
teachings.link: More than 130 years before the tickling recordings, Darwin noticed the same thing. He took it as a sign that humans and other apes are one family.

science.text: All the great apes, humans included, make laughing sounds in play and when tickled.
Laughter probably began in the shared ancestors of the great apes, millions of years ago.

other_view.view: They say we should not be too quick to call an ape's pant a laugh, or to say the ape feels what we feel. A pant may be a signal that means 'this is play', and we should check each feeling by what the ape does next.

practice.title: One laughing breath
practice.say: Sit up straight. Breathe in slowly through your nose. Now let it all out as a laugh: ha ha ha ha, until the breath is gone. Feel your tummy squeeze. Now sit very still and breathe quietly three times. A chimpanzee somewhere in a forest is laughing too, right now.
practice.kid: Sit up straight. Breathe in slowly. Let it out as a laugh: ha ha ha. Feel your tummy squeeze. Now sit still. Breathe quietly three times.

ask: A chimpanzee laughs breathing out and in. You laugh breathing out. Is it the same laugh, or a different one?
